title: Caring Well at Both Ends of Life (with Jen Wilkin)
summary: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor.
content: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor. They discuss how our culture’s prioritization of self-sufficiency poorly prepares us for the day when we’ll need to accept help. They share their stories of caring for aging parents and talk about how they’re seeking to number their own days aright as they age. Resources Mentioned: Dust to Dust by Jen Wilkin We Shall All Be Changed by Whitney Pipkin Being Mortal by Atul Gawande Related Resources: 5 Ways to Honor an Aging Loved One (Even When It’s Hard) The Joy of Caring for Aging Parents Caregivers Suffer from Dementia Too Honor Your Father and Mother Discussion Questions: 1. Have you ever cared for someone during a season of significant need, or have you received that care? How did the experience shape your understanding of dependence on others? 2. Why can it be difficult to receive help from others, even when we know we need it? What does our reluctance to depend on others reveal about us? 3. Our culture often measures a person’s worth by his or her productivity or abilities. How does the gospel challenge those assumptions, especially as we age? 4. When we think about the possibility of losing some of our independence and abilities as we age, what truths about God and our identity in Christ give us hope? 5. How can churches help ensure that older adults (especially those without children or nearby family) are known and cared for? 6. What practices or habits do you want to cultivate to help you age well, both physically and spiritually?
author: Courtney Doctor, Melissa Kruger, Jen Wilkin

title: Lessons from Ezra on Leading a Story You Didn’t Start
summary: Ezra entered a story God had already begun. Ezra teaches leaders how to continue God’s work in the lives of his people.
content: In the book of Ezra, Ezra doesn’t even appear until chapter 7. That means more than half the book unfolds before the man for whom it’s named ever steps onto the scene. That observation stayed with me long after our sermon series in the book ended. The more I reflected on it, the more it resonated with my experience of leadership. Ezra isn’t a leadership manual; the book’s primary purpose is to highlight God’s sovereignty and his steadfast commitment to carrying out his redemptive purposes in and through his people. But if we pay attention to how God uses Ezra in his ministry context, there is a word here to those called to lead stories they didn’t start. Story Ezra Entered Long before Ezra arrives, the Jewish exiles hear about the possibility of homecoming through King Cyrus’s decree, fulfilling the Word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah (chap. 1). Stirred by the Spirit, they leave the lives they had grown accustomed to and journey home to Jerusalem (chap. 2). The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem begins, and when its foundation is completed, the exiles’ pent-up emotions erupt into shouts of joy and sorrow that could barely be distinguished from one another (chap. 3). Unexpected opposition then halts the rebuilding (chap. 4), but through a series of providential circumstances, the work resumes, and the temple is finally completed after a long journey of uncertainty (chap. 5–6). This story is already filled with so many layers: stirring of the Spirit, risk, courage, failure, emotions, disappointment, uncertainty, sovereignty, grace. Every chapter seems to beg for more stories to be told. The point is simple yet profound: Before Ezra ever leads, God is already at work. A story is already underway. Ezra 1–6 isn’t an extended introduction, as though everything before chapter 7 were simply a prelude to Ezra’s ministry. Rather, in God’s timing, Ezra is brought into a story far larger than himself. The same is true for many leaders today who inherit a story they didn’t start. Every church carries memories of joy and sorrow, faithfulness and failure, growth and disappointment. Every congregation has a history that inevitably shapes its present. Wise leaders recognize that they aren’t beginning God’s work; they’re joining it. Story Ezra Continued What, then, can Ezra show us about leading a story we didn’t start? Here are four lessons. 1. Pray first. When King Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to guide and teach God’s people who have returned to Jerusalem, Ezra prepares to enter this story by calling those traveling with him to fast and pray. Rather than relying on military protection to get him safely to Jerusalem, he turns to trusting in God’s provision and protection (chap. 7–8). Notice how quickly Ezra turns to prayer. Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Do you have a habit of praying? Pause often and pray something even as simple as this: “Lord, go before me and help me join where you are and what you’re doing.” Prayer reminds us who is ultimately going before us to build up his people. 2. Expect heartbreak. In Ezra 9, after beginning his teaching ministry and seeking spiritual renewal among the people, Ezra learns that God’s people have fallen into serious covenant unfaithfulness. His response is surprising: He tears his garments, pulls out his hair, and falls before God. His first response isn’t outrage: Why is this happening now? I just started my new role! It’s not damage control: How bad is the situation, and what are my immediate action items? And it’s not blame shifting: This problem predates me. Thank God I’m not responsible for this! Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Ezra’s instinctive and immediate response is grief. Many leaders enter into new churches and ministry contexts hoping to teach, mentor, cast new vision, and build something impressive and influen
author: Benjamin Bae

title: When Families Sit Together in Church: The Missional Opportunity
summary: The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity.
content: Most pastors I know are working on a common problem: How do we better serve the people who come to church and feel like everyone has a family group and no one is genuinely welcoming? In a recent article , Dave Moore argues that for the sake of the Great Commission, you should stop sitting with your family at church. He writes that “church is for others” and says we should think of our church attendance in terms of deployment for mission. The article appeared on The Gospel Coalition’s Australian site. TGC’s international coalitions have their own independent editorial teams. All agree to publish resources that align with TGC’s Foundation Documents , but individual writers , staff members , and Council members often disagree on matters that fall outside our Confessional Statement and Theological Vision for Ministry. In this case, I respectfully disagree with Moore. Any church committed to reaching lost people and including outsiders is asking themselves how to best address the problems of cliques and people not feeling like they belong. But when Moore says that “dividing ourselves for the sake of others is the most beautiful picture of Christian unity,” I believe he overstates his case. The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. More than that, to present family members worshiping together as an obstacle to love for others neglects the mission of the family and God’s call to parents. Acknowledging legitimate situations where families can’t or don’t sit together in church, as Christians, we don’t choose between our families or our mission. Building gospel-centered families is Great Commission ministry. Families as Mission God commands parents to teach his words and ways diligently to their children (Deut. 6:7). We’re called to train up our children in the way they should go (Prov. 22:6). The Bible places a priority on the family as a first-order love over against providing for others (1 Tim. 5:8). The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. The primary responsibility for showing children “the way they should go” belongs to the parents, not the people of God in the abstract (Gen. 18:19). Parents set the tone for the worshipful commitment of a household (Josh. 24:15). Parents are the generation that proclaims the works of God to the next generation (Ps. 145:4). When Moore writes that “church is special spiritual-family time,” he neglects another reality: The primary disciple-making responsibility for children in those spiritual families is given to nuclear families—namely, mothers and fathers. Modeling worship for your children is ministry. It’s a blessing for your children to watch you week after week learning from God’s Word and participating in the life of the church. It’s good to make people feel welcome at church—and that includes children. To be entrusted with children is to be entrusted with the mission of God: the passing of God’s worship from one generation to the next. Families on Mission At the same time, it’s good to be intentional about those who come into the church without a family, without community, without certainty that anyone cares about them. That’s true for our approach to lone believers, and it’s true for our approach to the lost. So how can we address that problem without treating the family like an obstacle to engaging the isolated? 1. Loving families can be welcoming families. The best path forward for engaging people alone at church isn’t by neglecting an essential commitment—the family—but by leveraging the family as a unit for mission. It’s not “Sorry kids, someone else is more important.” Instead it’s “Hey kids, this is our new friend. She’s going to sit with us today.” My wife and I have worked to show our kids not that others come before them but that others come with us because we love to include people in our lives. As Jen Oshman says , “We will never sacrifice our family for the mission; but we will sacrific

title: Beyond the Battlefield: Veteran Suicide and the Value of Life
summary: On Veterans Day, we celebrate the willingness of those who have served and are serving to sacrifice for our country.
content: “We’ll teach you how to kill. When you get back, you’re the VA’s problem.” That’s what they told my old team sergeant before he deployed to Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division. The risk of killing or being killed is an inescapable part of military service. In the Army, recruits go through a formation process in Basic Combat Training that turns them into soldiers. Part of this means learning that the mission always comes first, which in turn must mean they’re expendable. First aid is taught with the assumption that at some point, someone will need a tourniquet, chest seal, or body bag. After all, the enemy also learns to shoot, and sometimes the mission requires soldiers to get into harm’s way. That’s part of the tragic necessity of war. No one would have followed Washington across the Delaware or left the landing craft on D-Day if staying alive were the number-one goal. A commander’s ability to orchestrate force in combat would break down with a military unwilling to die. But this same dynamic that makes militaries potent threatens the lives of those who fight, through the tragedy of veteran suicide. Necessity of Sacrifice We must understand sacrifice as more than mere operational necessity: Something is lost when nothing is worth dying for. C. S. Lewis famously warned of the danger of making men without chests—of a people without an anchoring morality to mediate the carnal passions of the stomach and the cold calculations of the head. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character, to say nothing of its national defense. Americans ought to be thankful that thousands of young men and women regularly sign the dotted line to join the armed forces, volunteering to put their country’s well-being ahead of their own. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character. The willingness to sacrifice that makes a military effective can carry a hidden cost. What happens when a soldier learns to put his life second, then struggles to understand its value when the mission ends? A soldier who was prepared to take a bullet downrange may think little of a bottle of whiskey, a pack of cigarettes, or opening up his motorcycle on the highway. When the Mission Ends Those who make it back from combat alive aren’t entirely safe. Veterans take their own lives at roughly twice the rate of the general population. Veteran suicide stems from a number of factors, including post-traumatic stress, moral injury, difficulty transitioning to civilian life, loss of purpose and social connection, traumatic brain injury, pain, and proximity to firearms. Alongside these factors, we should consider what it means to spend years learning to put one’s life second and what happens when that lesson outlasts the mission. There’s an obvious tension when it comes to the value of life. Christians know that our lives in this world aren’t ultimate (Rev. 12:11). Christians can face death because we recognize this life’s limits, while still treating life as a gift worthy of protection. As Jesus taught, being willing to die for others is the highest form of love (John 15:13). This is why the second person of the Trinity stepped down from heaven, took on the form of a servant, and obediently followed the Father’s mission orders to death on the cross (Phil. 2:6–8). Yet Jesus didn’t throw his life away; he demonstrated perfect courage. Between the foolhardiness that leads to blood on the highway and the cowardice that keeps men in hiding when a wolf growls at the door, stands courage. As G. K. Chesterton observes, “Courage is almost a contradiction in terms. It means a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die.” We see this in Christ’s agony in anticipation of the cross in the garden of Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). Yet he carried his cross anyway. Value of Life and Virtue of Sacrifice The Christian worldview ties together the value of both life and sacrifice,

title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. Local believers jumped into action with a meal roster. Costa Rican friends translated our English updates to equip our Spanish-speaking friends to pray. title: On Christmas, God Shook Up the World
summary: Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants.
content: Read For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. (Hag. 2:6–7) Reflect When this prophecy came to Haggai in 520 BC, did anyone imagine that God would shake up the world with a baby born to humble parents in Bethlehem? Or that “a little while” would be more than 500 years later? Yet if Advent teaches us anything, it’s that the Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. His timeline may not align with ours, but in the passage of centuries we experience his mercy. We read in 2 Peter 3:9, “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” The Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. In Hebrews 12:26, the writer expands on this relationship between patience and judgment by quoting Haggai 2. The shaking is a kind of sifting, like the sand separated from jewels in a strainer. The Lord shakes the world to sift out anyone who doesn’t worship that baby born in Bethlehem. Because even as a helpless babe, he is the King of kings and Lord of lords who will reign forever. In Jesus we see “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” the One who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). One day, after a little while, that baby would grow up and exercise his power in the most unexpected way. He would submit to death, even on a cross. The day he died on Calvary, the temple curtain was torn in two. An earthquake shook the city. Rocks split at the Place of a Skull (Matt. 27:32, 51). That helpless man, bloodied and beaten, commanded more authority than anyone else had realized—including the power to judge his judges. The Roman officer who commanded 100 confessed, “Truly this was the Son of God!” (v. 54). Those who don’t follow suit will be sifted. But the shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. By this sacrifice, believers will receive a “kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb. 12:28). To this kingdom all the treasures of the nations will accrue, as Haggai foresaw with the temple filled by God’s glory. God did this for the Hebrews when he delivered them from slavery. They plundered the Egyptians (Ex. 12:36). And he’ll do it again when he delivers the world from death, as the kings of the earth bring their glory to the temple in the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21:24). The shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. These kings will follow a path already trod by the wise men of the east, who tracked the star to baby Jesus. From the nations they brought their treasures—gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The purported king, Herod, could only see a threat. But these wise men fell down and worshiped the baby still nursing with his mother, Mary (Matt. 2:11). Do you see the power and the glory concealed from the world while contained in that baby? Do you see in him a King whose love for sinners kept him nailed to the cross? Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants. Advent is enduring an unstable world with hope because an unshakable kingdom is coming—in a little while. Respond How might the Lord’s seeming lack of action express his patience for you? How could you help your non-Christian friends and family see the glory in Jesus this Advent season?
author: Collin Hansen

title: Midlife Is a Crossroads, Not a Crisis
summary: In ‘Good News for Midlife,’ Jared Wilson reminds us to embrace our midlife crossroads, find new meaning in service to others, and let this season be an opportunity to discover grace upon grace in Jesus.
content: Last year, I was sitting with an early twentysomething grad student in our church. He said he was looking for an older man to mentor him, and I started thinking through our godly, wise men in their 50s and 60s. He stopped me and clarified: He was asking me to mentor him. “Wait, you think I’m old?!” I’m 42, and to be fair, I’ve been told I’m an “old soul” my whole life. Some have wondered aloud if I was born old. While I still don’t feel old, I’ll admit this new and strange season has spurred me to go looking for wisdom. I’ll tell you, reading about midlife is depressing. According to studies, happiness in life follows a U-shaped curve. Our self-reported happiness starts high in childhood, then decreases into adolescence and further into early adulthood. It bottoms out somewhere around age 46—smack in the center of middle age—before beginning to rise again and steadily increasing into our twilight years. Further, studies have shown that depression and anxiety also are highest around the age of 45. Despite all the bad news, Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace was encouraging. Writing from his early 50s, Jared Wilson, associate professor of pastoral ministry at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, understands the challenges of midlife but also provides refreshing hope for those of us finding our own way through. Understand Midlife Most definitions place “middle age” as 40 to 60, but it’s probably more accurate to describe midlife in terms of its demands and responsibilities. For me, it looks something like this: I still feel energetic, but it takes far longer to recover from lost sleep, injuries, and travel. My kids are now teenagers, and some days, I only see them for a half hour. Our grocery bill is three times our first mortgage. Our parents are in their 70s and now need more support from us than we need from them. I think I’m still in touch with modern culture, but my kids assure me I’m not. I may have 40-plus years left, but it sure feels like most of my life is now behind me. Most deeply, I’m frequently reflecting on life’s disappointments and griefs, wondering if I should have done this or that differently. This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Wilson, who writes specifically for men entering or inhabiting these decades, acknowledges all these challenges. “But,” he writes, “while this season presents unique challenges . . . midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing” (xi). Thankfully, Wilson helps us reframe the demands and opportunities of middle age not as a necessary crisis but as a critical crossroads . Crossroads, Not Crisis For almost 60 years, pop culture has made “midlife” nearly synonymous with “crisis.” The phrase comes from psychoanalyst Elliott Jaques’s 1965 essay “ Death and the Mid-Life Crisis ” and has been repeated across dozens of books ever since. (There’s even a board game called Mid-Life Crisis, where players aim to accumulate wealth and avoid landing on bankruptcy, divorce, and nervous breakdown.) This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Fortunately, recent studies suggest fewer than 20 percent of Americans experience a full-on crisis in these middle decades. Despite this, many of us face a unique temptation to flee from responsibility or forge some entirely new life. Wilson puts it poignantly: “Whether you’re in a crisis or not, at midlife you’re at a crossroads” (16). At this crossroads, we see down one path the allure of individualism and freedom from responsibility. We might simply call this path the road of empty promises. As the proverbs say, it seems right, but in the end, it leads to death (Prov. 14:12). The second path is one of embracing reality, stepping deeper into relationship, and trusting the goodness of God. This road offers no promises other than the hardships of real life. But it’s also where
author: Jeremy Linneman

title: Avoid the Trap of Bitterness
summary: Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps.
content: Imagine the people closest to you betray you. It’s your trust in them that lets them get close enough to hurt you so terribly. Now, imagine that this betrayal completely upends your life for years . Everything that made your life good—your family, your home, your safety—is violently taken from you. Now imagine years bleed into decades. Your life spirals into ever more pain and isolation. And every jab of hurt leads you to agonize over the initial wound: None of this would have happened if it weren’t for them. How could they do this? However, in the last few years, your fortunes have turned around. From the slums, you’re suddenly lifted to a vaulted position of power. People no longer take advantage of you but try to stay in your good graces. It doesn’t wash all the bitter memories away, but it’s something. And then, lo and behold, who happens to come before you but them . Your cruel betrayers are there, groveling, asking you for help. How would you feel? What would you do? If you haven’t picked up on it yet, this is the story of Joseph from Genesis. Sold into slavery by his brothers, Joseph walks through much injustice and suffering before being catapulted into the most powerful office in Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. And when his brothers come cringing toward him in the end, certain that Joseph will use his power to pay them back, Joseph responds with unexpected mercy, generosity, and warmth (Gen. 50:15–21) . How? Joseph avoids the trap of bitterness. And you can too, if you follow these three steps. 1. Understand Bitterness Bitterness is revealed in our emotions (coldness, anger, resentment, suspicion, revulsion), but it begins in our will. We choose bitterness when we believe that for justice or fairness to be preserved, the offender must be punished in some way. We may even claim to forgive, but in our heart of hearts, we fear that forgiveness comes at the expense of justice. So, you give your spouse the silent treatment, you cut your parents off, you make life difficult for your kids. Joseph avoids bitterness by trusting that God is the One who takes care of justice. When his brothers beg for mercy, Joseph replies, “Do not fear, for am I in the place of God?” (Gen. 50:19). Joseph knows it isn’t his place to deal out the judgment only God can give. The first step in avoiding bitterness is letting God take care of final justice (Rom. 12:14–21). Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Which is why we’re commanded unequivocally to repent of bitterness, full stop (Eph. 4:31). We’re never told bitterness is an acceptable method to coerce repentance or pursue justice, or is permissible until the other person apologizes and makes restitution. Reconciliation requires two people who are willing. But to repent of bitterness only requires one. Bitterness feels like a solution to the problem, but it isn’t. It’s trying to solve one sin with another sin. Bitterness isn’t the path to justice—only to more bitterness. Using bitterness to pursue justice is like using a hatchet to build a house, confident it’ll work just like a hammer. 2. Unmask Bitterness We’re called to be so absolute and unqualified in rejecting bitterness because of its penchant to spread. It’s a “root” (Heb. 12:15) that will only grow and become more difficult to uproot as time goes on. Plucking up a sapling is easy; removing an oak tree isn’t. Soon, the bitterness you feel toward Person A will make you more prone to taking offense at Person B and more sensitive to Person C. Soon, you become an angry person who holds grudges. It’s a root that “defiles many.” Bitterness is hard to detect initially because it hides so effectively behind a mask of morality. The bitter person “blesses himself in his heart, saying, ‘I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart’” (Deut. 29:19). In other words, “I’m not wrong, they are! They’re the ones who hurt me!” It not only immediately puts you into a

title: Build a Culture of Evangelism
summary: Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss how pastors can build a culture of evangelism by modeling gospel conversations, equipping church members to share their faith, and making evangelism a natural part of church life.
content: How can pastors help their churches become more evangelistic without relying on another program? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan discuss what it takes to build a culture where sharing the gospel becomes a normal part of church life. Mack Stiles The Gospel and Personal Evangelism by Mark Dever Out of the Saltshaker and into the World by Rebecca Manley Pippert The Art of Asking Better Questions by J. R. Briggs If you’re ready to go deeper, Southern Seminary’s PhD program is where that begins. Visit sbts.edu/phd to learn more.

title: Train Women to Teach the Bible: A 4-Week Plan
summary: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. But where do we find teachers?
content: Bible studies are the heartbeat of women’s ministries in many churches. More and more churches have come to prefer live teaching over video studies . But this can present a challenge for women’s ministry directors: Where do we find teachers? Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. Whether women have never taught the Scriptures before or are building on previous experience, we can help them grow and gain confidence in “rightly handling the word of truth” (2 Tim. 2:15) through careful instruction and practice. To equip women in my church to teach, I helped develop a four-session course. Here’s how we developed and implemented this training. Get Organized I first recruited two women with experience teaching the Bible, and together we prepared ourselves as instructors by taking the online Simeon Trust First Principles for Women course. We then personalized the principles we learned to fit our training goals for other women in our church. Since there are different strategies for approaching various genres of Scripture, the first time we held this course, we chose to train women on how to teach an epistle. We selected 1 Peter as our text and assigned each group a passage to work on throughout the course. For example, Group 1 had 1 Peter 1:1–12, Group 2 had 1:13–21, and Group 3 had 4:12–19. We used 5:1–11 as a common passage that we studied as a whole group. In subsequent courses, we chose other genres of Scripture: narrative using passages from a Gospel and wisdom/poetry using a psalm. Bible teachers don’t come ready-made. We have to raise them up through training. We promoted the training with a clear purpose: to help participants grow in their ability to understand and teach God’s Word. We spelled out our expectations: attending all four sessions, completing homework, and teaching a 10-minute message to peers. Individual attention in training is key, so we assigned each participant to a small group of three to six women with a leader. The leader gave feedback on homework and answered questions. Teach the Course Here’s what we covered each week, including teaching content, small-group work, and homework assignments. Week 1: Foundations of Study After sharing two foundational truths about the Bible—Scripture is God-breathed (2 Tim. 3:16–17) and Scripture is alive and active, changing us as we study it (Heb. 4:12)—we taught three principles. First, we never add to or subtract from what’s written in the Word (Deut. 4:2; 1 Cor. 4:6; Rev. 22:18–19). A Bible text isn’t a jumping-off point to give our insights. We must be diligent to stay faithful to the Holy Spirit’s intended meaning. We strive to “stay on the line” of Scripture , never going above it by adding to it (which can result in undue speculation or legalism) or going below it by taking away from it (avoiding unpleasant or confusing passages, or altering the meaning to what we want it to mean). Second, the Bible is one big story, with one Hero of the story (Luke 24:27). From Genesis to Revelation—creation, fall, redemption, and restoration—we see God at work to reconcile people to himself. The Old Testament points to our need for and anticipation of a Savior, and the New Testament records and reflects on that Savior. Understanding this one big story helps reveal the significance of each passage. Third, context is king and questions are key . Context is the setting in which something occurs, and it always guides our interpretation. We consider both the literary context (what comes before and after a passage) and the historical context (the situation in which the original audience found themselves). To “stay on the line,” asking in-depth questions of the passage is vital, so we introduced the participants to questions for an epistle . In small-group time, we had each woman read the group’s assigned passage aloud because a thoughtful reading aids understanding, as does hearing the passage multiple times. title: When Morningness Is Confused with Godliness
summary: Could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical?
content: “Do your quiet time with God every morning.” “Give God your first hours (your best hours!) of the day.” “Rise early for Scripture and prayer; it sets the tone for the rest of your day!” From pulpits to podcasts, I’ve heard these sentiments often in Christian circles. The instructions aren’t just to spend alone time with God but to specifically do so as the very first act of your day. For many, the “morning quiet time” has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. Actor Mark Wahlberg once went viral on Instagram for a screenshot of his morning routine : waking up at 2:30 a.m., praying at 2:45, and completing his first workout before 5:30. This is one of many examples of how early rising has become associated with aspirational godliness. But is it really more virtuous to be a morning person than a night owl? What If You Have to Sleep In? Behind the modern mindset of hyperidealized mornings is the assumption that being a “morning person” is a virtue in and of itself—a gritty choice toward wellness and productivity within everyone’s power. The implication is that if you’re disciplined and wise, you’ll set the alarm clock and start the day early; you’ll make it happen. If you’re slothful or foolish, you won’t. Extenuating circumstances are just excuses. For many, the ‘morning quiet time’ has become a measuring rod of how well you’re doing in your relationship with God. But what would this mean for nurses whose work begins and ends when it’s dark outside? What about parents with newborns, whose babies’ demands don’t abide by our ideal rhythms? How about Christians who are naturally night owls: most alert, focused, and productive at night? Should these folks just suck it up and aspire to get up earlier in spite of their circumstances? Or could it be possible that our idealizing of morning quiet times is more cultural than biblical? God Loves Early Risers At first glance, it might seem that God’s Word does value our mornings most. Pastor David Mathis wrote an insightful article summarizing the abundance of instances in Scripture in which God’s people (including Christ himself!) either rose early to good effect or were directed by God to do so. Consider the Psalms: In Psalm 5:3, David says, “O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice.” In Psalm 88:13, the Sons of Korah sing, “In the morning my prayer comes before you.” In Psalm 90:14, Moses prays to God, “Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.” God clearly meets with his people in the morning. Case closed? Not quite. When you consult the whole counsel of Scripture, it becomes clear that God emphasizes meditating on his Word, singing his praises, and praying to his name just as much in the night as in the morning. Nocturnal Worship Let’s explore some nighttime examples. In Acts 16:25–26, after Paul and Silas are imprisoned in Philippi, God’s Word notably mentions the timing of their worship: “About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God . . .” Silas and Paul don’t try to go to sleep early so they can engage with God at the crack of dawn. They stay up late, worshiping at midnight. The results are profound. In Psalm 63:5–6, David prays to the Lord, “My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night.” This psalm as a whole is arguably a nighttime prayer. David prays these lyrics to the Lord seemingly all while on his “bed,” singing midnight praises. Consider Jesus’s earthly life. On the fateful day before his crucifixion, when it comes to spending devoted time alone with his Father, Jesus prays passionately, in Gethsemane, at night (Matt. 26:36–56). There is no mention in the Gospels of Jesus rising early on this momentous day; it might have happened, but the recorded emphasis is Jesus’s spiritual devotion in the dark. Morning and evening aren’t

title: Contend Without Being Contentious
summary: In an age marked by theological compromise and unnecessary outrage, we need church leaders who can do more than win arguments.
content: “How do we contend for the faith biblically without becoming quarrelsome and contentious?” A member of my (Barry’s) congregation posed this thoughtful yet difficult question when our church was studying the letter of Jude. In his purpose statement (vv. 3–4), Jude says he wants to write about the salvation he shares in common with his recipients. However, he finds it necessary instead to exhort them to “contend for the faith.” What does obeying this exhortation involve? Before we contend for the faith, it’s essential to clarify how to approach confrontation and why we’re seeking to confront in the first place. Knowing myself, I (Ben) can have many sinful and unhelpful reasons for confronting; my pride often tempts me to seek my glory in confrontation rather than seeking the Lord’s glory. Yet when our motivation is wrong, our manner is too. Then, contending can quickly become contentiousness. Jude gives us a better way. Why and How To Confront His letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. Jude provides four basic confrontation categories that will help us defend the truth without becoming quarrelsome. 1. Oppose deceivers (v. 4). We must be able to distinguish between those who are confused and those who are deceivers. Not everyone who errs is a malicious false teacher. Some simply need patient guidance, instruction, and compassionate discipleship. Jude’s letter provides a framework for Christians to discern when we should confront error, and with what level of intensity. But others actively promote error, refuse to submit to biblical authority, or sow seeds of division that can lead God’s people away from Christ. Jude has deceivers in mind as his primary concern in his letter. He’s concerned not just that they’re in error but that they’re influential. For that reason, he wants the church to have the Spirit-led courage to confront the deceivers’ errors. Such contending requires wisdom. For pastors, it can involve correcting false teaching both privately and publicly. You may need to warn your church about dangerous influences or refuse to give a platform to those who persistently distort the gospel. Remember, Paul instructs elders to rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine (Titus 1:9) and to protect God’s flock from spiritual wolves (Acts 20:28–31). He also warns congregations to watch out for divisive teachers (Rom. 16:17–18). When we confront deceivers, our aim isn’t to embarrass them or to win arguments. Rather, we contend for the faith because truth matters and because Christ’s church matters. 2. Instruct doubters (v. 22). In the Christian life, we encounter many who have doubts about the faith. They know the truth, but they struggle to believe it. Instructing those who doubt may not seem like contending for the faith at first, but gently clearing up their concerns strengthens both their faith and the church’s faith. Contending well for doubters can prevent them from wandering or even from becoming deceivers. It’s an act of mercy (v. 22), and it must be done mercifully. When believers doubt or begin to waver on the truth, our responsibility isn’t to ruthlessly force truth on them. We also shouldn’t ignore their questions. Neither response is merciful. Instead, we must engage doubters’ questions with compassion, trusting that the Lord will reveal truth to them in his time. Our belief in Scripture’s sufficiency is critical here. God’s Word, not our teaching or apologetic skill, possesses the power to reveal his truth. Doubts are many and various, but the Bible remains constant and trustworthy. 3. Warn wanderers (v. 23). Between doubting and deceiving stands another category: wandering. Some in the church drift, or have drifted, toward dangerous doctrinal error or patterns of sin that, if left unchecked, will lead to their fall. Jude prescribes the appropriate response: “Save others by snatching them out of the fire” (v. 23). His imagery conveys urge

title: Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya
summary: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. Somali-based al-Shabab militants ambushed Christian construction workers inspecting a road project. The workers, who were non-locals, were targeted because of their identity and faith. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to…   The post  Al-Shabab Kills 5 Christians in Mandera, Kenya  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On the morning of Nov. 10, gunfire shattered the quiet along the Mandera-Arabia road in the Hagarsu area of Mandera County, Kenya. Somali-based al-Shabab militants ambushed Christian construction workers inspecting a road project. The workers, who were non-locals, were targeted because of their identity and faith. A driver and the two police reservists assigned to protect them were also killed. Eight people in total were killed, with the attack following a pattern of al-Shabab-linked violence in Kenya’s northeastern borderlands. “The attack was swift but intense, leaving many traumatized, but even though we walk through the valley of the shadow of death, we will fear no evil, for Jesus is with us; His rod and staff, they comfort us,” an eyewitness said. “That’s where we draw our confidence from regardless of the present circumstances.” A Persistent Danger Mandera County lies along Kenya’s border with Somalia. For Christians living in the region, insecurity is a reality. Christians who move into the area for work are vulnerable. Churches operate under constant threat; believers travel cautiously, pastors limit evening gatherings, and congregations often worship with one eye on the door. Even traveling to work can expose Christians to danger. “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; but Jesus said, ‘I have come that they may have life, and have it to the full,’” a local church leader said. “We are becoming more vigilant and yet committed to the preaching of the gospel in the face of this constant threat from the Islamic fighters.” Always a Target Al-Shabab has repeatedly targeted Christians in the northeastern region, particularly those perceived as outsiders and those who do not share the group’s extremist religious ideology. Converts from Islam to Christianity remain especially vulnerable to intimidation, threats, and violence. The police reservists assigned to protect the workers also lost their lives. “The word of God declared that we should not grow weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up,” an eyewitness who wished to remain anonymous said. “We therefore bury the dead and comfort the widows, but we refuse to stop gathering in his name and preaching the gospel of salvation.” Responding to the killing of the five Christians, another church leader requested prayers and support for the believers in Mandera and the families of the victims. “We call upon the global church to stand with persecuted believers in Kenya and pray for the families of those killed, the wounded, and Christians across Mandera,” he said. “Pray for the protection of Christian workers, pastors, and congregations, and that they will have the courage to continue worshipping and sharing the gospel. Pray for lasting peace. The church in Mandera is not forgotten. Let us stand with them.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis
summary: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more…   The post  At Least 26 Killed in DRC’s Mambasa Territory Amid Ebola Crisis  first appeared on  International Christian Concern
content: Twenty-six people have reportedly been killed and several others abducted in a new attack carried out by the Islamist rebels of Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) on Nov. 10, during the night, in Mambasa territory, Ituri province, northeastern DR Congo, a country where nearly 93% of the population is Christian. According to a local association coordinator, Malikidogo, more than six villages were affected, including Kangwayi, Misele, Mingazi, and Mambaka. “The situation is very serious; we identified 26 people killed, several others abducted, and many families are still searching for their missing loved ones,” Malikidogo said. “Aside from the death of many people, five houses were burnt alongside some motorcycles. We are calling on the authorities to take urgent action to protect the population.” Left With Nothing Survivors who succeeded in escaping reported that many families had to run for their lives, leaving their homes and belongings behind. “We were very afraid when we realized that the enemies were already in the village when we heard people crying and others running in every direction,” one survivor said. “We just fled without having time to collect our belongings, just to save our lives. We do not know what will happen next, and we are afraid that they might come and reach Mambasa city where we are today.” The attack comes at a difficult time for local communities, which are already facing the threat of Ebola . Residents are now dealing with both the fear of the disease and the danger of further attacks. There are concerns that the violence could also make it harder to control the Ebola outbreak. People fleeing their villages may spread the disease to other communities, while insecurity could prevent health workers from reaching those who need medical help. A local leader also expressed concern about the situation and called for stronger protection of civilians. “We have suffered for many years because of the atrocities committed by ADF Islamist terrorists,” he said. “We are already struggling with Ebola, and now we are facing these attacks again. We cannot continue living like this. We are calling on the government and security forces to protect our communities before more innocent lives are lost.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: 4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre
summary: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again…   The post  4 Killed Days After Cantine Massacre  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Just days after the deadly massacre in Cantine, where at least 33 civilians were reportedly killed, suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) fighters have struck again in Beni Territory, claiming four more lives and burning several houses in Mabalako, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. At about 12:20 a.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, Mabalako once again faced ADF violence , with a fresh overnight attack in the Kamahume neighborhood. According to local civil society representatives, the death toll rose from an initial three to four, while more than seven houses were also set ablaze during the deadly incursion. The attack has renewed fears among civilians already traumatized by the violence that struck Cantine-Aloya less than a week earlier. The proximity of these two attacks in time and location has heightened concerns about the continuing threat posed by the ADF to civilian populations across Beni. “We are living in constant fear,” said Mulwahali, a survivor. “We have not yet recovered from the pain of what happened in Cantine, where innocent people were brutally killed and homes reduced to ashes. Now the violence has reached Mabalako, and once again we are mourning our loved ones and watching our homes burn. We do not know who will be next or where these attackers will strike again. We are even tired of burying our people without heads. All we want is to live in peace and sleep in our homes without fearing that we may never see another morning.” A Need for Security Local civil society representatives have appealed to security services to take full responsibility for protecting civilians, strengthen security operations, and prevent further attacks. Residents of Runzayi, Malondo, Ngazi, and Kibunamaru have also been urged to remain vigilant, maintain calm, and cooperate with security forces by reporting suspicious movements. “We cannot continue living at the mercy of armed attackers,” a local Catholic bishop said. “Although the intervention of the FARDC helped limit the destruction in Mabalako, the fact that the attackers could strike and disappear without their direction being known leaves us deeply frightened. We want security, not another massacre.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . For interviews, please email us . title: The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage
summary: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After…   The post  The Girl They Killed for Refusing a Forced Marriage  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 6, an 18-year-old Christian girl named Ajak Mabior was beaten to death in Jonglei, South Sudan, after refusing to enter a forced marriage arranged by her family. She was expected to marry an older Muslim man — a marriage she opposed because of her Christian faith and her unwillingness to be forced into it. After attempting to escape, she was killed by her own brother and cousin. Days later, police in Bor arrested the two men but released them without charges after family members demanded their freedom, arguing that “there was no case” because they were relatives. A Common Problem The killing has raised serious concerns among Christian leaders about the pressure Christian girls face when their faith and personal convictions conflict with family expectations. “When a young girl is killed for refusing a forced marriage, and the killers walk free because they are family, the message is clear: Tradition is stronger than the law, and stronger than the value of a life,” a local pastor said. “Many of our Christian daughters live under this same shadow.” For Christian girls in South Sudan , forced marriages can become a matter of religious persecution when they are pressured to marry outside their faith and abandon their Christian convictions. Those who refuse may face rejection, threats, intimidation, and violence from their own families. Mabior’s death highlights the vulnerability of young Christian women who seek to remain faithful to Christ while facing pressure to submit to marriages that violate their faith and conscience. “The church teaches that every life is precious because it is created in the image of God,” the pastor added. “Yet when a Christian girl refuses a marriage that would bind her against her will, she can be treated as a traitor to the community. We have buried too many who paid that price.” Seeking Justice The authorities’ response has added to the church’s concerns. Police reportedly released the suspects without the consent of the Jonglei State Caretaker Commissioner. The justification that the suspects were relatives raises serious questions about the protection available to Christian girls facing forced marriages and violence. When perpetrators are released without facing justice, vulnerable Christian women are left with little confidence that the authorities will protect their right to practice their faith and make decisions according to their conscience. “We preach freedom in Christ, but our young people still live in fear of the consequences of that freedom,” the pastor said. “If the police and local authorities remain quiet, the church becomes the only place left where these girls and boys can find a voice. We need courage to speak, and we need the wider Body of Christ to stand with us.” Mabior’s case raises concerns about forced interfaith marriages, religious pressure, and violence against young Christian women in South Sudan. “We call on the wider Body of Christ to pray for Ajak’s justice, and for the protection of Christian girls facing forced marriages because of their faith,” an International Christian Concern (ICC) staffer said. “Pray that the church will have the courage to speak against religious coercion and violence, and that the authorities will uphold the law and protect vulnerable believers.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians
summary: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government…   The post  Ansaru Militants Claim Killing of Muslim Cleric Who Preached Peace with Christians  first ap
content: Ansaru militants have claimed responsibility for shooting dead a Muslim cleric known for promoting peaceful coexistence between Christians and Muslims, raising fresh concerns about the threats facing religious voices who challenge extremist ideologies in Nigeria. Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka and his friend, Adamu Abubakar, were killed Monday evening, Oct. 26, in Dutsin-Ma Local Government Area of Katsina state. Two armed men riding a motorcycle reportedly opened fire on the men outside the cleric’s residence before fleeing. The Nigeria Police in Katsina confirmed the killing. The Nigerian government condemned the killings on Tuesday, while Ansaru subsequently claimed responsibility in an audio message, accusing Masussuka of being an infidel and opposing Islam. Masussuka had used social media to share Islamic teachings in Hausa, a major language spoken across northern Nigeria. In some of his videos, he called on Muslims to stop describing Christians as infidels and urged followers of both religions to live together peacefully. His message challenged religious hostility at a time when Christian communities in parts of Nigeria continue to face deadly attacks from armed extremist groups. For Christians who heard his teachings, Masussuka’s appeal for coexistence offered a reminder that resistance to religious hatred can also come from within the Muslim community. His killing has raised questions about whether those who challenge extremist interpretations of religion can safely express their views. Ansaru Accuses Cleric of Opposing Islam In an audio message released Tuesday, Oct. 27, Ansaru claimed it attacked at about 8:30 p.m. The speaker reportedly referred to Tuesday as the day of the killing, although the deaths were reported to have occurred on Monday evening. The group’s description of Masussuka as an infidel is significant because the cleric had reportedly used his platform to challenge the practice of labeling Christians in that way; the accusation against him raises concerns about the risks faced by people whose religious teachings conflict with extremist beliefs. Masussuka’s friend, Abubakar, was killed in the same shooting. Publicly available information about Abubakar’s life, his relationship with the cleric, and whether the attackers specifically targeted either man remains limited. Their deaths have left two families grieving and a community seeking answers about why the men were killed. Ansaru, formerly known as Jama’atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis Sudan, is a Nigerian jihadist organization that emerged as a breakaway faction of Boko Haram around 2012. The group has longstanding links to al-Qaida in the Islamic Maghreb, an al-Qaida affiliate active in the Sahel and North Africa. Ansaru has been associated with kidnappings, hostage killings, and attacks against security personnel and other targets. The United States designated the group a Foreign Terrorist Organization in 2013. Ansaru is one of several armed extremist organizations operating within Nigeria’s wider security crisis. Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) have carried out attacks on Christian worshippers, churches and predominantly Christian communities, as well as killings of Muslim civilians and others they consider opponents. These groups are distinct, and responsibility for each attack must be established through evidence. Nevertheless, their activities have contributed to a climate in which religious communities fear violence, displacement and the loss of loved ones. For Nigerian Christians, the danger extends beyond individual killings. Attacks on communities, places of worship and religious leaders can disrupt church activities, force families from their homes and leave survivors struggling to rebuild their lives. title: Desperation, Fear Grow as Malaysia Clamps Down on Freedom of Conscience
summary: A wave of viral social media videos featuring Malaysian citizens publicly declaring their departure from state-sanctioned Sunni Islam has cast a harsh spotlight on the severe lack of religious freedom in the Southeast Asian nation. While state authorities have scrambled to investigate and suppress the footage, international religious freedom advocates warn that the phenomenon…   The post  Desperation, Fear Grow as Malaysia Clamps Down on Freedom of Conscience  first appeared on  International Ch
content: A wave of viral social media videos featuring Malaysian citizens publicly declaring their departure from state-sanctioned Sunni Islam has cast a harsh spotlight on the severe lack of religious freedom in the Southeast Asian nation. While state authorities have scrambled to investigate and suppress the footage, international religious freedom advocates warn that the phenomenon highlights a much deeper, systemic crisis: the complete criminalization of apostasy for ethnic Malays and the intense persecution faced by those who desire to follow other faiths, including Christianity. Under Article 160 of the Constitution of Malaysia, all ethnic Malays are legally defined as Muslims. This constitutional binding leaves no legal avenue for a Malay individual to officially change their religion. For those who experience a personal crisis of faith or choose to embrace Christianity, the path forward is fraught with state-sponsored surveillance, social ostracism, and severe legal penalties. Central to this machinery of suppression is the powerful federal agency JAKIM (Department of Islamic Development Malaysia) and state-level enforcers like JAIS (Selangor Islamic Religious Department). Together, they operate a rigid, dual-track legal system where Shariah courts hold near-absolute jurisdiction over Muslims. Requests by individuals to officially exit Islam are systematically rejected. Instead of granting freedom of conscience, JAIS and other state bodies actively weaponize mandatory detention in state-run Islamic rehabilitation centers (pusat pemurnian akidah). These centers function as forced re-education camps. Converts who are caught or who attempt to petition the courts for apostasy are routinely sentenced to months of involuntary confinement. Inside, they are subjected to intense psychological pressure, isolation, and compulsory doctrinal lectures designed to break their resolve and force a recantation. Recently, JAIS publicized a court-ordered Istitabah (forced repentance ritual) for a social media figure, signaling that the state will use its full administrative weight to enforce religious compliance. Recent landmark legal battles from 2025 and 2026 expose a devastating reality: born-Muslims face a structural wall of total rejections. In an Oct. 2, 2025 ruling, the Federal Court — Malaysia’s highest civil judiciary — completely shut down a final appeal from a 47-year-old Christian convert who spent years fighting the Shariah court system just to return to his original faith following a divorce. The apex court reaffirmed that civil courts have zero jurisdiction to override Shariah rejections, leaving the believer legally trapped. Similarly, on Jan. 6, 2025, a Selangor woman who was unilaterally converted to Islam as a child saw her final legal challenge collapse at the Federal Court, cementing the precedent that her state identity card (MyKad) must permanently brand her as a Muslim. Even elderly believers who have secretly practiced their faith for decades are being hunted through bureaucracy. In June 2026, a 58-year-old mother filed a prominent judicial review against the National Registration Department (JPN) after they flatly refused to remove the “Islam” label from her identification card — despite her having formally converted out of Islam via a deed poll more than 30 years ago. JPN continues to trap her under state custody, demanding a clearance letter from the Shariah court that officials refuse to grant. The statistics highlight how tightly the trap is wound. Historical data shows that out of 863 formal applications submitted nationwide to leave Islam during a 10-year period, only 168 were granted. Legal analysts emphasize that nearly 100% of those rare exceptions were administrative clerical corrections in East Malaysia — such as a Jan. 7 Kota Kinabalu High Court ruling where a father and three children successfully proved they were raised Christian and that an NRD officer had made a data-entry error. The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) stormed Cantine in the Madiwe sector of Beni territory, in the North Kivu Province during the night of Thursday, Nov. 5, into the early hours of Nov. 6, leaving civilians dead, homes…   The post  More than 30 Killed in Latest ADF Attack  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Fear, bloodshed, and devastation have once again descended upon communities in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) stormed Cantine in the Madiwe sector of Beni territory, in the North Kivu Province during the night of Thursday, Nov. 5, into the early hours of Nov. 6, leaving civilians dead, homes burning, and an already vulnerable population gripped by terror. Justin Paluku, president of the Civil Society Forces Vives of Madiwe, confirmed that the provisional death toll stood at more than 30 civilians. “For families that went to bed hoping to wake up to another ordinary morning, the night turned into a nightmare of unimaginable suffering,” Paluku said. “We are deeply concerned about the safety of our population. Christian Civilians cannot continue living like prisoners in their own communities, constantly wondering when armed men will strike again. Our people deserve protection, peace and the freedom to live without fear.” Seeking Safety As news of the attack spread, residents began fleeing Cantine toward neighboring areas considered relatively safer. Children, women, and the elderly are among those facing the uncertainty of displacement, leaving behind homes, livelihoods, and personal belongings. For Christian survivors, the immediate concern is no longer what tomorrow will bring, but whether they will survive another attack . “We heard the sounds of violence, and fear immediately took control of us,” a survivor of the attack said. “We had no time to collect our belongings. All we wanted was to escape with our lives. We have lost our sense of security, and we do not know whether we will ever return to our homes again.” The reported burning of homes and looting of property represent more than material destruction. They strip Christian families of their dignity, deepen their vulnerability, and leave children exposed to hunger, insecurity, and psychological trauma. The wider Beni region has endured years of repeated attacks, killings, abductions, and displacement attributed to armed groups, particularly the ADF. Each new incident adds another painful chapter to the suffering of communities that continue to demand protection and justice. To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . content: On Nov. 6, Titus Hassan Malika stood with his classmates and received his diploma — a quiet but powerful moment marking the end of a long, difficult road. The Sudanese Christian, who fled violence and persecution in his homeland, had received support from International Christian Concern (ICC). With God’s help, what once seemed impossible had become reality. “The support I received from ICC is a dream come true,” Malika said. “I never imagined that someone would stand with me for so many years, believing in my future when I could barely see it myself. This graduation is not only my achievement — it is the fruit of their faithfulness and God’s provision.” Titus grew up in Sudan, where following Jesus grew increasingly dangerous . As pressure on Christian communities intensified amid conflict and targeted hostility, he was forced to leave everything behind. With little more than his faith, he crossed into Kenya as a refugee, carrying the weight of loss, uncertainty, and the hope that God still had a future for him. By His Side In 2023, ICC stepped into that uncertainty. Through consistent support, practical help, encouragement, and the means to continue his studies, we walked with Titus through years of hardship. The path was not easy. He faced the daily challenges of life, the lingering trauma of persecution, and the enduring discipline of education while far from home. Yet he pressed on. “Jesus Christ has been the center of my life from the day I fled Sudan until this moment,” he said. “When I had no home, he was my shelter. When fear tried to silence me, he gave me courage. Every step of this journey has been possible only because he walked with me and never left me alone.” As he steps into his next chapter, Titus carries both a Bachelor’s degree in business administration and management, as well as a testimony that God can bring beauty from ashes, and that the Body of Christ, when it stands with the persecuted, can help rewrite a life marked by suffering into one marked by grace. “I give thanks to God for ICC, for they have been the hands and feet of Christ to me,” he said. “As it is written, ‘And my God will meet all your needs according to the riches of his glory in Christ Jesus’ (Philippians 4:19). Truly, the Lord has done this. May he continue to bless those who have poured out their lives so that I could stand here today.” To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: Father Nearly Kills Children for Following Christ
summary: On Nov. 3, Kabugho Kasfa and Muhindo Ashraf endured a horrific attack after their father discovered their decision to follow Christ. Their father instantly attacked them after he heard them singing a Christian song. “He became as dangerous as a lion and started beating us with heavy blows,” Kasfa said. “I could not bear watching…   The post  Father Nearly Kills Children for Following Christ  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: On Nov. 3, Kabugho Kasfa and Muhindo Ashraf endured a horrific attack after their father discovered their decision to follow Christ. Their father instantly attacked them after he heard them singing a Christian song. “He became as dangerous as a lion and started beating us with heavy blows,” Kasfa said. “I could not bear watching him choke my brother, almost to the point of death. I became terrified and began screaming for help, fearing that he might take our lives. Knowing that I would attract the attention of Christians, he wanted to tie our mouths with a cloth. I had no choice but to bite him to save my life.” Ashraf’s journey to Christianity began at his school in Mpondwe, Uganda, where he attended chapel services and interacted with Christian classmates. Through the chapel teachings, he learned about the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, which sparked his interest in understanding the Christian faith. However, biblical teachings were not the only influence. The kindness and conduct of his Christian friends also left a lasting impression. “Dad always taught us to hate non-Muslims and view Christians as our enemies, but ever since I started school, my experiences have been completely different,” Ashraf said. “The Christian students have welcomed me with such genuine kindness and friendship that it is making me seriously reconsider everything we were raised to believe.” As Ashraf continued learning about the gospel, he became convinced that Jesus was God and that he wanted to surrender his life to him. He eventually accepted Jesus as his Lord and Savior and shared his newfound faith with his sister, Kasfa, who also decided to follow Christ. Nowhere to Turn Their decision, however, came at a terrible cost. Kasfa recounted how she watched in terror as their father beat them and choked her brother. Fearing for their lives, she screamed for help until some Christians heard their cries and rushed to their rescue. They helped the siblings escape and took them to a hiding place. The ordeal left the two young converts without a home or their family’s protection. Having already lost their mother, they now found themselves rejected by the very person who was supposed to protect them. “We had already lost our mother, and now the very person who was supposed to protect us was hurting us and driving us away,” Kasfa said. “We have nowhere to go and do not know where we shall spend the night.” Although Uganda’s constitution guarantees religious freedom, reports of violence against converts are fairly common. Muslims comprise no more than 12% of Uganda’s population, with most concentrated in the East. Despite everything they had endured, Kasfa thanked the Christians who had come to their rescue. She acknowledged that they did not know what would have happened to them if nobody had heard their cries. She added that they had only wanted to follow Jesus Christ, but that decision had cost them their home and the protection of their family. To read more news stories, visit the ICC Newsroom . title: No Arrests After Muslim Gunmen Kill 6 in Plateau Attacks
summary: Suspected Muslim Gunmen killed at least six people, including a Nigerian soldier, in separate attacks on communities in Plateau state, Nigeria. The attacks occurred on Sunday night, Nov. 8, in Bel village, Sho community, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area (LGA), and Lakas community in Panyam, near the Mangu-Pankshin border in Mangu LGA. Four people, including…   The post  No Arrests After Muslim Gunmen Kill 6 in Plateau Attacks  first appeared on  International Christian Concern .
content: Suspected Muslim Gunmen killed at least six people, including a Nigerian soldier, in separate attacks on communities in Plateau state, Nigeria. The attacks occurred on Sunday night, Nov. 8, in Bel village, Sho community, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area (LGA), and Lakas community in Panyam, near the Mangu-Pankshin border in Mangu LGA. Four people, including three civilians and a soldier, were reportedly killed when gunmen stormed Bel village at about 9 p.m. and opened fire. A resident of Bel village, Bulus Bot, who confirmed the attack to International Christian Concern (ICC), said several people also sustained gunshot injuries. The attack forced residents to seek safety as gunfire rang through the community. He said the attackers are Islamic Fulani herders who want to take over their land. Rwang Tengwong, publicity secretary of the Berom Youth Moulders Association (BYM), confirmed the killings and identified three of the civilian victims as Emmanuel Pam Dachung, 15; Joseph Gyang, 28; and Emmanuel Yohanna, 32. The soldier has not been publicly identified. According to a six-year study conducted by the Observatory for Religious Freedom in Africa (ORFA), Islamic Fulani militias are by far the deadliest persecutors of Christians in Nigeria. The network of militias is responsible for four times more civilian deaths than the two prominent Islamic terror organizations, Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), combined. The study’s findings challenge the commonly held belief that the two organized terror groups kill the larger number of Christians, highlighting the Fulani network’s expanded efforts to target Christians. A Second Attack Two additional people were reportedly killed in a separate attack on the Lakas community in Panyam, bringing the reported death toll from the two incidents to at least six. “Muslim Fulani stopped us from going to the farm to harvest our crops, and we are now afraid to go to the church to worship,” Mathias said. “Nigerian authorities failed to protect us.” Tengwong told ICC that no arrests had been made following either attack. He specifically accused the Nigerian Army of failing to apprehend any of the suspected Fulani attackers. Tengwong condemned the killings and called on security agencies to identify and arrest those responsible, warning that the failure to apprehend attackers could leave surrounding communities exposed to further violence. Residents and eyewitnesses alleged that Fulani extremists carried out the attacks, targeting predominantly Christian communities. Some residents described the assaults as part of a pattern of violence aimed at taking over ancestral lands and forcing indigenous populations from their communities. These allegations could not be independently verified. The latest attacks add to continuing reports of armed assaults against rural communities in Plateau, particularly in Barkin Ladi, Bassa, Riyom, and Mangu local government areas, where Christian farming communities have repeatedly reported killings, destruction of property, displacement, and threats to their livelihoods.
