title: Pertolongan yang Tidak Pernah Terlambat
title_zh: 永远不会迟到的帮助
content: Oleh: Odysius B. Temara Bersyukur untuk kasih karunia Tuhan yang selama ini tidak henti-hentinya saya rasakan dalam kehidupan saya. Pada kesempatan kali ini, saya ingin berbagi tentang kisah pengalaman hidup saya. Semasa kuliah, saya merasa bahwa saya adalah salah satu orang yang paling beruntung karena hampir selalu mendapatkan kemudahan dalam studi saya. Saya mendapatkan dosen-dosen yang ramah, teman-teman yang selalu mendukung saya, bahkan para staf akademik yang sangat bisa diajak bekerja sama. Semuanya berjalan sesuai dengan apa yang saya rancangkan sampai tiba-tiba segalanya berubah ketika saya menginjak semester akhir. Saya sangat terkejut ketika mengetahui bahwa saya diberi dosen pembimbing yang terkenal sangat sulit untuk penulisan skripsi saya. Beliau adalah salah satu dosen yang paling sibuk dan paling susah untuk dihubungi, terlebih untuk konsultasi. Pernah sampai tiga minggu beliau keluar kota, sakit, dan terlalu sibuk dengan tugas-tugas mengajar sehingga skripsi saya menjadi terbengkalai karena saya tidak bisa berkonsultasi dengan beliau. Ketika saya sedang berkonsultasi dengan beliau, sering kali beliau juga menyelipkan kalimat-kalimat sarkastik yang terkadang membuat saya lebih tertekan lagi. Seiring berjalannya waktu, teman-teman saya mulai lulus satu per satu, dan saya masih terjebak. Pada saat itu, saya merasa sangat kesal karena skripsi saya tidak kunjung selesai. Bukan karena saya yang malas-malasan, tetapi karena sulitnya menemui dosen pembimbing saya. Saya sempat mempertimbangkan untuk pindah pembimbing, tetapi rasanya sangat sayang kalau harus mulai dari awal lagi. Saya menceritakan keluh kesah saya kepada orang tua saya. Ayah saya menyarankan saya untuk lebih giat lagi berdoa, serahkan semuanya kepada Tuhan. Saya berdoa kepada Tuhan supaya Dia melembutkan hati dosen pembimbing saya dan juga memberi kekuatan dan kesabaran untuk saya dalam menghadapi beliau. Hari demi hari, saya berdoa dan sedikit demi sedikit tampak mulai terjadi perubahan pada sikap dosen pembimbing saya. Perubahan sikap itu tidak hanya terjadi kepada saya, tetapi juga kepada anak bimbingannya yang lain. Akhirnya, dengan proses yang cukup panjang, saya berhasil menyelesaikan skripsi saya dan lulus pada 12 Agustus 2014. Meskipun rancangan saya gagal untuk bisa lulus dalam 3,5 tahun, saya merasa bersyukur karena pertolongan Tuhan tidak pernah terlambat bagi saya sehingga saya masih bisa lulus tepat waktu. Sampai sekarang, saya senantiasa mengucap syukur kepada Tuhan atas segala yang Tuhan izinkan terjadi dalam kehidupan saya. Saya menyadari bahwa seberat apa pun permasalahan hidup yang saya hadapi, tangan kuat Tuhan akan selalu ada untuk menuntun saya melewatinya.

title: Merasakan Kasih Natal
title_zh: 感受圣诞节的爱
content: Natal merupakan liburan yang paling istimewa bagi ayah saya. Persiapan menjelang Natal, berbelanja hadiah, dan menghias rumah tidak membuatnya lelah - bahkan ia sangat menikmatinya. Ibu bercerita, ayah memperkenalkan saya dengan pohon Natal saya yang pertama waktu saya masih berusia sembilan hari. Pohon Natal itu kecil, tetapi setiap hiasan, lilin, dan untaian perada perak digantungnya dengan sangat teliti pada tempatnya, seolah-olah hanya ia yang dapat melakukannya. Setelah selesai, ayah mengangkat saya dari keranjang buaian dan menggendong saya supaya melihat hasil pekerjaan tangannya. Ayah masih menghias empat pohon Natal sesudah itu dan setiap kali pohonnya lebih besar dari tahun sebelumnya. Pada hari ia meninggal -- tak lama setelah menderita radang paru-paru -- ibu duduk dengan saya membicarakan Natal. "Madeline," katanya lembut, "Sinterklas akan memberikan hadiah untukmu, tetapi kita tidak mempunyai pohon dan hiasannya. Tahun ini pengeluaran kita sudah terlalu banyak." Besok hari Natal, tetapi sampai pagi ini tidak ada persiapan khusus untuk keesokah harinya, selain kebaktian pagi dan makan malam di rumah salah seorang anggota keluarga. Menjelang sore, telepon berbunyi dan ibu mengangkatnya. Tidak lama kemudian saya mendengar ibu berkata, "Anda baik sekali, tetapi rasanya kami akan melewatkan malam Natal di rumah. Natal ini pertama kali sejak ..." Lalu ibu dapat melanjutkan lagi, berterima kasih kepada penelepon itu sekali lagi dan menutup pembicaraan. "Siapa Bu?" tanya saya. "Salah seorang tetangga kita," kata ibu. "Ia mengundang kita malam ini. Ibu ... Ibu tidak bisa." Ibu diam saja hampir sepanjang hari. Sorenya, ibu berubah pendapat. Ia menelepon tetangga kami, mengatakan kami akan mampir sebentar. "Dia baik sekali," kata ibu kepada saya, "dan kita tidak mau dianggap tidak menghargainya." Setelah kami membunyikan bel pintu rumah tetangga kami, nyonya rumah menyambut dan mencium kami, lalu mengantar kami melewati serambi. Ruang tamu kelihatannya gelap, tetapi anehnya ada cahaya yang berwarna-warni. Ia mengajak kami masuk, dan saya melangkah ke dalam ruangan dan terperangah. Di sana, di tengah taburan lampu yang berwarna-warni dan bermacam-macam hiasan, lengkap dengan hadiah-hadiah yang dibungkus dengan kertas wama-warni yang cerah, berdiri sebuah pohon Natal yang indah sekali. Di sekeliling pohon itu duduk Ny. Abrams, Ny. Cohen, Ny. Blount, Ny. Dreyfus, sambil tersenyum lebar. "Selamat datang!" sapa mereka serempak. Sampai sekarang saya dapat memejamkan mata dan mengingat kisah tersebut dengan jelas. Sering ingatan itu menguatkan saya apabila keadaan memburuk, waktu saya meragukan hati manusia. Saya masih dapat merasakan kasih tetangga kami -- kaum ibu Yahudi yang mengambil risiko untuk melaksanakan tradisi yang tidak mereka kenal supaya seorang anak Kristen yang sudah tidak mempunyai ayah tetap dapat bergembira merayakan Natal. - Madeline Weatherford | Dipublikasikan | : | http://natal.sabda.org |

content: L’événement a marqué son temps. Le 28 octobre 1926, Pie XI sacrait évêques six prêtres chinois dans la basilique Saint-Pierre. Des prêtres spécialement venus à Rome pour leur ordination afin de marquer leurs liens et leur fidélité au siège pétrinien. Ces sacres marquaient alors une véritable volonté missionnaire et l’espoir d’un christianisme d’expansion en Chine. Dès Léon XIII, l’Église eut la volonté de former un clergé local, autochtone, pour favoriser la vivacité des Églises particulières et ne pas donner l’impression que la christianisation était le bras armé de la colonisation. En novembre 1919, Benoît XV publia un premier texte d’envergure avec la lettre apostolique Maximum illud. Le prêtre autochtone y est présenté comme « merveilleusement adapté à instiller la foi » dans le cœur de ses compatriotes. Pour le Pape « on ne doit pas former un clergé indigène de classe inférieure » : la formation du clergé autochrome doit être solide et identique à celle du clergé européen. summary: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que termi
content: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que terminé en el 92, fue sobre catolicismo y política en la Argentina”. Y hay más: “Debo mi fe a la Iglesia Argentina, leyendo artículos de monseñor (Gustavo) Franceschi, volví a la fe”, dice. Ese conocimiento de nuestro país y de su fe mayoritaria representó una ventaja a la hora de escribir sobre Bergoglio, ya que cada etapa de la trayectoria del futuro Papa está debidamente contextualizada en la época que atravesaba el país. Desde aquel marzo de 2013, cuando la novedad de un pontífice argentino y jesuita impactó al mundo entero, Ivereihg siempre pensó que vendría cuando Francisco visitara la Argentina, viaje que finalmente no se concretó. “Ahora vengo con León”, comenta. En efecto, este escritor, historiador, periodista y analista de asuntos religiosos y políticos estará en nuestro país contemporáneamente con la visita del papa León XIV, invitado por la Universidad del Salvador (USAL), donde dictó, el pasado viernes 6, una clase magistral sobre “El giro latinoamericano Francisco-León: la Iglesia misionera sinodal y el cambio de época”. Ivereigh también es co-autor de Let Us Dream (Soñemos Juntos, 2020), un libro escrito en colaboración con Francisco. Su trabajo más reciente es First Belong to God: On Retreat with Pope Francis (Lo primero es pertenecer a Dios: Un retiro con el Papa Francisco, 2024), basado en los escritos y charlas de Bergoglio como director espiritual de un retiro ignaciano de 8 días. De 2004 a 2006, Ivereigh fue colaborador del entonces arzobispo de Westminster, cardenal Cormac Murphy-O’Connor, uno de los más activos promotores de la candidatura de Jorge Mario Bergoglio al papado. Ivereigh considera que el papado de Francisco inició un giro latinoamericano hacia una iglesia misionera y sinodal, cuyo primer paso fue la exhortación apostólica Evangelii Gaudium (noviembre de 2013), sobre “el anuncio del Evangelio en el mundo actual”, con la cual, dice, “Francisco inaugura una hoja de ruta de su Papado que también es la del pontificado de León”. Pero esa hoja de ruta tenía una génesis anterior: el ya famoso documento de Aparecida, la V Conferencia General del Episcopado Latinoamericano y del Caribe (Celam), redactado por Bergoglio. De esta manera, “América Latina pasó a ser la iglesia fuente”, señala, porque “siempre hay una parte de la Iglesia de la cual brota un dinamismo teológico”. Antes, ese rol lo cumplía Europa, pero a partir del Concilio Vaticano II eso cambia porque es en América Latina donde mejor se lo pone en práctica. Aclara que “fuente” no quiere decir centro; de hecho, “Francisco quería una Iglesia multipolar”. — ¿Hasta qué punto Aparecida refleja a Bergoglio como individualidad y hasta dónde es la Iglesia latinoamericana, que usted define como “fuente”? — El proceso de preparación de esa conferencia general, fue muy sinodal, de mucha consulta, y el papel de Bergoglio en esa conferencia general es muy conocido. Creo que influyó la recepción del Concilio Vaticano II en el Río de La Plata, que tuvo un matiz distinto al resto de América Latina. Tal vez, cuando llegó a Aparecida esa visión sobre la religiosidad popular estaba ya madura. Es decir, una teología de espiritualidad latinoamericana, distinta a anteriores teologías latinoamericanas. Bergoglio tenía muchas cosas que eran de él. Pero también llevaba en su forma de ser y de pensar muchos aportes de la iglesia argentina, la influencia de Lucio Gera y de Rafael Tello y toda esa tradición. — ¿Cómo vio el impacto de su papado en la Argentina? — Creo que una de las razones por las que no vino, sobre todo al principio, fue que tenía horror del triunfalismo. Y sabía que tal vez los argentinos tenían —todos los países lo tienen— una cierta tentación de decir: “El Papa es argentino”. title: Un progetto giovane per la Chiesa missionaria : Wecare .
summary: “Alla Chiesa universale, colonna e fondamento, il suo Fondatore ha affidato un duplice compito: di generare figli, di educarli e reggerli, guidando con materna provvidenza la vita dei singoli come dei
content: “Alla Chiesa universale, colonna e fondamento, il suo Fondatore ha affidato un duplice compito: di generare figli, di educarli e reggerli, guidando con materna provvidenza la vita dei singoli come dei popoli, la cui grande dignità essa sempre ebbe nel massimo rispetto e tutelò con sollecitudine”, scrive Giovanni XVI nell’enciclica “Mater et magistra”. Jorge Mario Bergoglio non aveva partecipato al Concilio, ma aveva “imparato” il Concilio in quel grande laboratorio ecclesiale che è l’America Latina. Da qui, perciò, la predisposizione, una volta Papa, a privilegiare le riforme pastorali rispetto a quelle istituzionali. Così come, dall’essere un gesuita, portato al pragmatismo, alla semplificazione, discendeva la sua contrarietà nei riguardi degli ideologismi, dei bizantinismi teologici, delle discussioni dottrinali che sapevano tanto di accademismo. E allora, tenendo conto di questo, si potrà facilmente capire perché il Papa Francesco, nella sua esortazione apostolica “Evangelii gaudium”, abbia disegnato il profilo di una Chiesa caratterizzata da una “conversione pastorale e missionaria”, capace di “trasformare ogni cosa”. Una Chiesa che deve “annunciare il Vangelo a tutti, in tutti i luoghi, in tutte le occasioni, senza indugio, senza repulsioni e senza paura”. Una Chiesa dove tutti possano sentirsi “accolti, amati, perdonati”. Una Chiesa povera tra i poveri, povera con i poveri. Il “sogno” bergogliano non faceva altro che riprendere il progetto riformatore del Vaticano II. Anche se ora formulato in termini nuovi, e provocatori, per come il Papa poneva l’urgenza di cambiare, di rinnovarsi, insomma, di essere cristiani in maniera autenticamente evangelica. Così come la lettura dei “segni dei tempi” andava al di là dello stesso metodo induttivo impiegato dalla “Gaudium et spes”: non si partiva più dal “centro” ma dalle “periferie”; non più dall’Occidente ma dal Sud, dalla tragica condizione dei poveri.

content: Dense fog blanketed our landscape on Nov. 1. The old timers say to expect some kind of precipitation 90 days from fog. That will be Feb. 1, 2027. Former pastor of the Lustre EMB Church, John Skillman, called to let our community know of the passing of Melody Nickel – Sharon's sister and wife of Missionary Dan Nickel – this morning in Ireland. Our deepest sympathies are extended to their families. Dan and Melody had been here in August as speakers of the recent Harvest Festival. They were long term missionaries in Ireland. Former LCHS teacher, Sarel Matthyser, passed away peacefully on Oct. 30, having lost his battle with cancer. He and his son, Josua had returned to South Africa to be with family. LCHS Foundation President Keith Unger emceed the Annual Foundation dinner. The LCHS Choir members served the meal of baked potatoes, brisket or barbecued pulled pork. Prizes were drawn and reports given. Keith introduced the speaker, Andy Shewey. He said the MB Foundation philosophy "is based on two principles: 1) God owns it all. (Ps 24:1) and 2) Therefore we are His stewards, seeking be rich in good works. (II Cor. 9:6-7, I Tim 6:17-19, Matthew 25)." He defined "heritage" as "something passed down from previous generations including cultural traditions, historical values, physical property and spiritual faith." Quoting David Green, CEO of Hobby Lobby, Mr. Shewey said "Legacy is what we set in motion." "Legacy is a last act of stewardship, reflecting your values, makes a statement and is a way to give past your own lifetime." He gave several family stories as examples of how generations were affected by how these people (in Kansas and Oklahoma) were "giving meaning to money." The evening was an encouragement to all who attended. The jamboree and junior high games of late have been exciting. The girls played Nashua at home Saturday evening, Frazer on Tuesday with Lustre Junior High girls winning in overtime by four, and on Friday travelled to Dodson to play the coyotes. The jamboree girls won 19-12, the jamboree boys lost 27-29 in a good game, the junior high girls won 31-18, and the junior high boys also won. The Frontier school comes Saturday to play at Lustre. Then it's Frazer and North Country next weekend, both at Lustre before the tournaments on Nov 20-21.

title: La Nación / La diócesis de San Lorenzo cuenta con nuevo obispo
summary: El papa León XIV nombró a monseñor Pierre Jubinville como nuevo obispo de la diócesis de San Lorenzo en reemplazo de monseñor Joaquín Robledo, quien presentó renuncia al cargo. La Nunciatura Apostólic
content: El papa León XIV nombró a monseñor Pierre Jubinville como nuevo obispo de la diócesis de San Lorenzo en reemplazo de monseñor Joaquín Robledo, quien presentó renuncia al cargo. La Nunciatura Apostólica en Paraguay comunicó el sábado 7 de noviembre que el santo padre aceptó la renuncia de Robledo y designó en su reemplazo a monseñor Pierre Laurent Jubinville, quien se desempeñaba como obispo de San Pedro y es el actual presidente de la Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya (CEP). La decisión fue anunciada por la CEP, conforme a lo establecido en el Código de Derecho Canónico, que contempla la renuncia de los obispos al alcanzar los 75 años de edad. No obstante, monseñor Robledo continuará al frente de la diócesis como administrador apostólico hasta la toma de posesión canónica de su sucesor. La Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya agradeció a monseñor Robledo por su servicio pastoral y dedicación a la Iglesia, al tiempo que encomendó en oración al nuevo obispo, deseándole un fecundo ministerio episcopal en su nueva misión. El nuevo obispo Monseñor Pierre Laurent Jubinville nació el 5 de agosto de 1960 en Ottawa, Canadá. Tras algunas experiencias laborales, ingresó en la Congregación del Espíritu Santo y estudió Teología en la Universidad de Montreal. Emitió los votos solemnes en 1988 y fue ordenado presbítero el 17 de setiembre de 1988. Tras algunas experiencias misioneras en África, realizó estudios académicos en Montreal y París. Llegó a Paraguay en 1991, desarrolló diversas tareas pastorales y formativas; entre ellas, se desempeñó en la pastoral indígena de la parroquia San José Obrero, en la Diócesis de San Pedro; fue párroco de San Francisco de Asís y formador de la Congregación del Espíritu Santo en Asunción. En 2013 fue nombrado obispo de San Pedro y recibió la ordenación episcopal el 21 de diciembre de ese mismo año. Además, ejerció la vicepresidencia de la Conferencia Episcopal Paraguaya entre 2018 y 2024 y, desde noviembre de 2024, ocupa la presidencia de dicha institución. La Diócesis de San Lorenzo comprende varias localidades del departamento Central, entre ellas Capiatá, San Lorenzo, Ñemby, Itá, Ypané, Guarambaré, Villeta, Nueva Italia, San Antonio, J. Augusto Saldívar, Ypacaraí y Thompson.

title: Pope warns of dehumanization caused by AI
summary: Pope Leo XIV waves to faithful from the popemobile upon his arrival for a prayer vigil at the Centenario Stadium in Montevideo on November 7, 2026. (AFP Photo) Pope Leo XIV warned students on Nov. 7 o
content: Pope Leo XIV waves to faithful from the popemobile upon his arrival for a prayer vigil at the Centenario Stadium in Montevideo on November 7, 2026. (AFP Photo) Pope Leo XIV warned students on Nov. 7 of “dehumanization” through the use of AI in education, and urged schools and university to place the “person before the algorithm.” “The process of dehumanization we are experiencing poses a challenge,” the pope, who has warned repeatedly about the need to ensure AI is used ethically, said in a speech at the Catholic University of Uruguay. Just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the 71-year-old pontiff is on a 12-day tour of South Africa where he served nearly two decades as a missionary. On Nov. 7, he visited the crime-blighted Montevideo neighborhood of Casavalle. The murder rate in the impoverished district is four times the national average and residents spoke movingly of the dangers they faced, like commonplace gun violence. Katherine Silva’s voice cracked with emotion as she told the pope about the violence and abuse she had suffered as a child. After ending up homeless at 15, the young mother said she “went through very dark times” and “nearly died.” “There are children in Uruguay who do not go to school for fear of never returning home,” Leo said. “In a country as rich in resources as this, children should never have to go to bed hungry... Much less should they have to suffer violence to the point of losing their lives,” he added. As police helicopters flew overhead, locals waved and cheered to welcome the head of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics, who blessed 12 new low-income houses financed by the Church.

title: Il Mimmo Beneventano a padre Zanotelli , Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista - Notizie
summary: Saranno assegnati a padre Alex Zanotelli, al giornalista Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista (consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista) i riconoscimenti dell'edizione
content: Saranno assegnati a padre Alex Zanotelli, al giornalista Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista (consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista) i riconoscimenti dell'edizione 2026 del 'Riconoscimento Nazionale Mimmo Beneventano', la cui cerimonia di premiazione è in programma sabato prossimo, 14 novembre, a Sasso di Castalda (Potenza). Ne ha dato notizia Libera Basilicata, ricordando che "il 7 novembre è una data che porta con sé una ferita ancora aperta, ma anche una testimonianza che il tempo non ha cancellato. In questo giorno del 1980, a Ottaviano, veniva assassinato dalla camorra Mimmo Beneventano, giovane medico, consigliere comunale e uomo impegnato nella difesa della propria comunità dalle infiltrazioni e dalle speculazioni della criminalità organizzata. Beneventano - è ricordato nel comunicato - aveva scelto di non voltarsi dall'altra parte, opponendosi apertamente agli interessi della Nuova Camorra Organizzata e pagando con la vita il proprio impegno. A distanza di 46 anni, il suo esempio continua a rappresentare un riferimento per quanti credono nella democrazia, nella libertà, nella giustizia sociale e nella necessità di contrastare ogni forma di sopraffazione mafiosa. È proprio nel segno di questa eredità civile e morale che sabato 14 novembre, a Sasso di Castalda, paese caro a Mimmo per le origini familiari e nel cui cimitero riposa, si terrà il XVIII Riconoscimento Nazionale Mimmo Beneventano, appuntamento annuale dedicato a valorizzare l'impegno di donne e uomini che, attraverso il proprio lavoro e le proprie scelte, contribuiscono ad affermare i valori della democrazia e della legalità contro le mafie e la corruzione". Per l'edizione 2026 "i riconoscimenti saranno assegnati a tre personalità provenienti da ambiti diversi, ma accomunate da percorsi di impegno civile e professionale. Padre Alex Zanotelli, missionario comboniano e giornalista, è una figura di riferimento nel panorama dell'impegno sociale e della cooperazione internazionale. Per anni ha vissuto a Korogocho, una delle baraccopoli di Nairobi, condividendo la quotidianità delle comunità più povere. È stato direttore della rivista Nigrizia e successivamente di Mosaico di pace, distinguendosi per la sua attività di denuncia e per le battaglie sui temi della pace, del disarmo, della giustizia sociale e dell'acqua come bene comune. Massimo Battista, al quale il riconoscimento sarà conferito alla memoria, è stato consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista. Ha legato il proprio percorso personale e pubblico alle vicende della città di Taranto, impegnandosi nelle questioni riguardanti il mondo del lavoro, la salute dei cittadini e la tutela ambientale. La sua figura resta legata alle battaglie civili e sociali del territorio tarantino. Leo Amato, giornalista, ha svolto una parte significativa della propria attività professionale in Basilicata, collaborando con Il Quotidiano del Sud, per poi proseguire il suo percorso anche a livello nazionale nella redazione de Il Fatto Quotidiano. Nel corso della sua carriera si è occupato di cronaca, politica e inchieste, seguendo da vicino vicende e questioni di interesse pubblico legate ai territori. Tre storie e tre percorsi che saranno al centro della cerimonia di quest'anno, nel solco dei valori che hanno contraddistinto la vita di Mimmo Beneventano". Riproduzione riservata © Copyright ANSA

title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
summary: By Mark Ellis — Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, […]  The post  Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Amber Sparks (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports. Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life. But there is one story she will never forget. It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel. At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls. Dropping in (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook) Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.” “The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.” Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.” Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.” So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.” She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.” It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight. It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef. “I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.” Another manta ray (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes. Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1) As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience. “I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’ Amber Sparks Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it. Then Amber got the sur

title: Houston’s Epiphanies: Turrell and Rothko

Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. content: The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. summary: While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. content: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did). But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics. In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing). Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange. However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available. That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.” It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31). After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation. It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”. He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord. When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands. Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US. The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer. On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race. As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.” The post WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp first appeared on God Reports .

title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
summary: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of […]  The post  In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star , the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article , following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years. Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present. Lewis was only eight years old. It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early. In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes: “You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.” For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow. A Life in Words Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s. He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone , where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture. Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing. Grover Lewis (ChatPGT) Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders: “At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…” There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world. Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent. Two Texans, Two Literary Paths Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word. Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions. Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life. content: Pastor Peter Colon portraying Major Rossvally in the movie of his story By Charles Gardner — A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65). Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life. But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain. Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah. Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah. Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life. Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears. He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole. But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14). So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.” A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel. He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father. In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city. An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64. A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online. content: By Charles Gardner — We used to be regular viewers of the The Great British Bake-Off TV series, now being screened on Channel 4, celebrating the efforts of amateur contestants in the kitchen. My wife is qualified in home economics and once, in her far-off student days, helped Mary Berry out over the weekend. I too like to lend a hand with my cooking skills. So when, the other day, we were intrigued to see how new presenter Nigella Lawson was doing on the show, we switched it on – and were truly appalled at the foul language spewing out of the mouths of at least two contestants. Taking the name of the Lord Jesus Christ in vain, they loudly expressed their frustration (rather than praise) at things going wrong with their concoctions in front of more than seven million viewers. We switched it off, vowing to complain in the strongest possible terms, which I have since done. And though it’s hard to be surprised at the language regularly heard on television programmes these days, I was shocked to the core by Channel 4’s response, basically saying that this particularly offensive blasphemy doesn’t come under the category of “strong language”. Really? It’s surely the worst of them all. “We are sorry to hear you were offended by some of the language used within the programme,” they wrote. “Whilst we do appreciate that you find the use of such phrases or words unacceptable, we are not obliged under the Ofcom code to obscure them, nor do they fall under the category for strong language. We therefore have no obligation to bleep them either pre- or post-watershed.” I had suggested that they could at least have edited them out, adding that they were being very hypocritical as they wouldn’t have allowed swearing in the name of Mohammed, a point which they ignored. Have we sunk so low in our nation that there is nothing left that is sacred, except woke left-wing ideology and appeasement of those who hate the God of Israel and his Son Jesus, our Lord? But we have forsaken the God who brought peace and prosperity to Britain, and who saved us from Nazi invasion, for the idols of food and celebrity. Shame on us! Is it not time the Christian world woke up and stood against this flood of filth in our midst, which will sweep us away into the oblivion of a third-rate country if we do not act soon. Where has the ‘land of hope and glory’ gone? The ‘mother of the free’ we sing about at the Proms, calling on the God ‘who made thee mighty’ to ‘make thee mightier yet’? The Apostle Paul was surely prophesying the decline and fall of the Roman Empire in his letter to the early Christians in Rome (a mixture of Jews and Gentiles), when he wrote: “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities – his eternal power and divine nature – have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made, so that men are without excuse.” (Romans 1:18-20) The post Offended by foul language on food show first appeared on God Reports .

content: By Mike Shreve — Tent meeting in the 80s Evangelism has been my focus for 55 years, ministering throughout the United States and in 14 other nations. God mercifully saved me during the Jesus Revolution (1970), out of a hippie lifestyle and a passionate, though misguided pursuit of truth through far eastern religious practices (yoga and meditation). Shortly after encountering Jesus and being delivered, along with another brother in the Lord, I began hitchhiking around the country, preaching the Gospel on street corners and college campuses. That developed through the years into ministry in churches, auditoriums, conferences, and tent crusades. Supernatural provision and divine intervention has always carried me, through every phase of this five-and-a-half-decade-long adventure. However, the following story is a classic. For about 25 years I carried big Gospel tents around the country. At the time of this “miracle,” I was transporting a 60’ x 90’ tent from one city to the next in an old, dilapidated bus that kept introducing new challenges to our amateur mechanic skills (putting it mildly). One day, on our way to Tampa, Florida—unfortunately—we hit a large pothole in the road that put a serious dent in the rear left rim on which a large truck tire was mounted. From that point, the inner tube would not retain air, making it necessary to stop every thirty miles or so to fill it up again . . . and again . . . and again . . . making the trip painfully slow. Adding to the problem, the other rear tire was bald, and we had no spare (couldn’t afford one). So, a flat would have brought us to a complete standstill. Sometimes, I think back on those days (when our zeal for the Kingdom outran any wisdom we might have possessed), and I marvel at the many times God took care of us anyway (like the loving heavenly Father that He is). Thousands of pounds of equipment were packed into that groaning, creaking, rusty, decrepit bus — heavy canvas tent sections, metal poles, stakes, platform, and 300 chairs—and only a few days allowed in between cities for transit and setup. No, we really could not afford any setbacks. And yes, a lot of “faith prayers” were uttered during every trip (or were they “presumptive proclamations”—not sure—maybe a mix of the two). An old split rim tire mounted on an old bus Once we got to Tampa, attempting to be frugal, I visited the junkyards hoping to find a used replacement rim. As if they had conspired to dissuade me, every junkyard owner/manager shot down my hopes with a similar assessment, “Fella, you won’t find one of them old split-rims anywhere. They’re dangerous. When you try to mount a tire on one, they can snap open and injure somebody real bad, cutting off a hand, even killing a person. We melted ‘em all down as scrap metal.” (Go ahead, look them up online—they were even called “widow-makers.”) It was the same story everywhere I went. Nobody could help. Then three weeks passed and we had to pack the bus and head to our next location—Bessemer City, North Carolina. It was a college-level, biblically-sound course on developing long-suffering and patience: stopping every thirty miles or so to air up that unpredictable tire, pleading with God to somehow supernaturally assist us in our journey by making sure none of the tires blew. Somehow, we made it—around 600 miles—stopping about 25 times. Then an incredible miracle happened! God did it and I still feel awestruck, just writing about it. As we turned into the fairgrounds area, right in the middle of the entrance were two brand new, neatly-stacked truck tires (unclaimed), exactly the size we used on the bus—mounted (you guessed it!) on the very same split rims our bus required. Talk about worshiping God—we launched into a praise session right then and there! What were the odds? We all knew it had to be God. content: By Charles Gardner — Barrie Clark painting of a Spitfire The Battle of Britain, which saw Spitfires and Hurricanes save us from Nazi invasion and ensure our freedom, apparently ended after three months on October 31, 1940. As we move past that date this year, many of us will no doubt be distracted by superficial celebrations like Halloween, more animated by the spectre of ghosts and witches than the real threats to our society from those who would rob us of our hard-fought freedom. Our present government would have us paralyzed with fear and trepidation as they urge us to stock up our cupboards in case of emergency, but Jesus reminds us how he takes care of the sparrows and urges us to trust him for all our needs. That wartime battle in the skies would not have been won without a nationwide turning to God in prayer, and the current challenges can only be overcome in the spiritual realm. For there is a ferocious war taking place in the heavenly places (see Ephesians 6:12) urgently requiring our participation. All these sentiments are being fuelled by our own government’s attitudes to Israel and by their cowardice in pandering to the prejudice of those whose votes they covet. title: Rejoice in the Lamb: Benjamin Britten, Christopher Smart, and the Poetry of Faith
summary: When music meets poetry, the result can be more than art, it can become an expression of spiritual wonder. The last time I heard Professor Bruce Redford speak about the eccentric British clergyman and poet Christopher Smart (1722–1771), I was so inspired that I included a substantial portion of Smart’s extraordinary poem, Jubilate Agno, in […]  The post  Rejoice in the Lamb: Benjamin Britten, Christopher Smart, and the Poetry of Faith  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: When music meets poetry, the result can be more than art, it can become an expression of spiritual wonder. Christopher Smart The last time I heard Professor Bruce Redford speak about the eccentric British clergyman and poet Christopher Smart (1722–1771), I was so inspired that I included a substantial portion of Smart’s extraordinary poem, Jubilate Agno , in my book Beauty (And the Banana) . I described Smart as a theopoet , someone whose deep religious convictions found expression through a distinctive and imaginative poetic vision. Smart was no ordinary poet. His writings moved freely between the sacred and the seemingly mundane, finding divine significance in everything from biblical figures to animals and the natural world. His poetry was exuberant, unconventional, and, at times, wonderfully strange. For Smart, creation itself was a chorus of praise, and every living thing had a part to play. Recently, I had another opportunity to hear Redford explore Smart’s remarkable literary legacy, this time through the music of British composer Benjamin Britten (1913–1976). As part of an All Saints’ Day concert at the Cathedral of St. John in Albuquerque, New Mexico, celebrating Britten’s music, Redford delivered a pre-concert lecture focusing on the composer’s Rejoice in the Lamb , a choral masterpiece that brings Smart’s unusual poetry to life. The evening offered a fascinating intersection of literature, music, theology, and history, demonstrating how two artists separated by nearly two centuries could share a common vision of wonder. The Musical Imagination of Benjamin Britten Benjamin Britten. Photo: Public Domain. Redford, a former professor at Boston University who was living in England when Britten died in 1976, identified three defining characteristics of the composer’s work. First, Britten’s music is distinguished by “passion and variety.” His compositions resist easy categorization, moving between emotional intensity, dramatic storytelling, and moments of remarkable spiritual intimacy. Redford described Britten’s approach as creating a kind of musical parable, pointing to Curlew River , one of Britten’s church parables, as a particularly compelling example. Second, Britten demonstrated an extraordinary ability to balance “economy and scope.” Redford compared this quality to the novels of Jane Austen, whose carefully constructed narratives reveal entire worlds through seemingly modest details. Similarly, Britten could communicate profound emotional and spiritual truths through restrained musical means. Nothing was wasted; every note served a purpose. Third, and perhaps most important for the evening’s performance, Britten possessed an exceptional “sensitivity to words.” Redford described him as an “inspired” interpreter of literary texts, a composer who understood that music should not merely accompany poetry but illuminate its deeper meaning. It was this third characteristic that led Redford to Christopher Smart. When an Eccentric Poet Meets a Brilliant Composer In 1943, Britten composed Rejoice in the Lamb (Op. 30), a festival cantata scored for four soloists, SATB choir, and organ. The composition draws its text from Smart’s Jubilate Agno , a work of religious poetry that remained largely unknown for nearly two centuries. Christopher Smart Smart wrote much of the poem during his confinement in a private madhouse in eighteenth-century London. Its unconventional structure, biblical references, exuberant language, and seemingly spontaneous declarations of praise made it unlike almost anything else in English religious literature. The manuscript remained unpublished until W. F. Stead brought it to public attention in 1939. Soon afterward, the poet W. H. Auden introduced Britten to Smart’s newly published work while the composer was living in the United States. The connection proved fruitful. Britten recognized something remarkable in Smart’s poetry: an unrestrained celebration of creation that could be translated into music.

content: By Charles Gardner — The watching world is holding its breath after record numbers of Israelis went to the polls. We perhaps need reminding that the Jewish state is the only democracy in the Middle East and has been on an almost constant war-footing since the last national elections four years ago. With all the regular ballots counted, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc leads that of ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot by 53-48 seats, with the Arab parties winning the remaining 19. That leaves the incumbent needing to persuade eight Arab members to make up the required 61-seat Knesset majority by joining him in a coalition. Negotiations are expected to take some time. Modern Israel has been under threat ever since her re-birth in 1948, but the situation is worse than ever since the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023 – the most severe attack on Jews since the Holocaust. As with Lebanon-based Hezbollah, the Hamas terrorists are backed by Iran, which has long vowed to wipe Israel off the map and is now reportedly very close to nuclear capability. All of which explains why the spectre of Iran hangs over the election like a ghastly Halloween ghost. ‘Bibi’ Netanyahu has even created an AI-generated image of Tel Aviv being struck by an atomic bomb. The nuclear threat is real, and the mullahs would love to vaporise the city’s large Jewish population (which includes many peace-loving Arabs). Netanyahu – who has led the country on and off for the past 30 years – is a firm and steady figure who can be relied upon to defend his country to the death, whereas some opposition candidates could be more accommodating to the demands of Western leaders for two-state solutions, though I doubt they will go that far as a Palestinian state in the midst of Israel is seen by many as signing a death warrant. However, former PM Ariel Sharon (another ex-military chief) effectively gave away Gaza in 2005 in a so-called ‘land for peace’ deal. And how did Gaza thank Israel? With constant attacks on their generous neighbours! In a nation surrounded by enemies, defence is obviously a major factor in policy making, but the irony is that military men (like Sharon) don’t always see things as clearly as the political sharpshooters. President Trump backs Netanyahu because “there’s a job to finish”, but Israel cannot afford to keep relying on allies, including America. Significantly, Bibi is a friend of evangelical Christians, repeatedly acknowledging their unstinting support while the world increasingly turns against them. This support is borne of biblical understanding of God’s long-term purposes for Israel who are not just fighting for their own survival. title: Jewish refugee became vicar
summary: By Charles Gardner — At a time when Hitler aimed to harm us, here was a German who came to bless us! Of Jewish heritage, he was sacked as a judge by […]  The post  Jewish refugee became vicar  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: Werner Simonson By Charles Gardner — At a time when Hitler aimed to harm us, here was a German who came to bless us! Holocaust survivor Werner Simonson escaped from Germany just before the outbreak of World War II, only to become a Church of England vicar. Of Jewish heritage, he was sacked as a judge by the Nazis and had to endure long years of separation from his non-Jewish wife and son before being reunited after the war. Like John Wesley who was rescued as a child from a rectory fire, Werner was also ‘a brand plucked from the burning’. He was about to be executed in a World War I battle with France when he and his colleagues were wrongly accused of shooting French prisoners. But just in time, one of the latter told the firing squad how Werner had treated him with kindness, even sharing his rations with him. The German soldier was thus spared but spent the next five years as a prisoner of the French, his POW status only ending in 1920 after being put to work restoring war damage in northern France. When finally released, it was a case of ‘from the frying pan into the fire’ as Germany was plunged into despair and division following their ignominious defeat. Despite this, however, Werner quickly rose to the status of high court judge before being dismissed from his post by the Nazis when they discovered his Jewish heritage. The fact that he had fought for Germany and had won the coveted Iron Cross for gallantry counted for nothing. And the increasing pressure of anticipating arrest led to a breakdown of his health. But while attending his niece’s confirmation at a Lutheran church, feeling at the end of his rope, it was as if the preacher was speaking directly into his desperate situation. He opened his heart to Christ and found new life and hope. “In the utter darkness which had engulfed my life I saw a new light,” he recalled.(1) He became associated with the Confessing Church opposing the Nazis’ antisemitic policies and was advised to escape which he managed to do with the help of the Bishop of Chichester Dr George Bell. Werner’s wife Leonie and son Juergen stayed behind but were able to join him after the war. Being German, he was initially interned with others on the Isle of Man where he led fellow Jews to faith in Christ. But tragic news followed, hearing of his father’s death, his mother being murdered in a concentration camp and his sister Ilse gassed in Auschwitz. Werner knew little English when he arrived on these shores but attracted much interest by being ordained at St Paul’s Cathedral when Britain was in the middle of a war with his fatherland. He was subsequently offered back the post of judge in the new West Germany along with a pension for the job from which he had been previously dismissed by the Nazis. But he turned down the generous offer. “I could not exchange service in the ministry of God for service in administering man-made law; accepting this offer would have meant abandoning God’s call to me, and this I could not do.” But this humble and self-effacing man was to make a significant impact in succeeding years as he proclaimed the gospel in three separate London parishes, ending up at St Luke’s, Hampstead, where (from 1956-1965) he helped yet more Jewish people to a knowledge of their Messiah. He continued passionately preaching Christ almost till his final breath in 1991, aged 101. 1 With grateful thanks to War and Grace by Don Stephens (Evangelical Press 2005), an imprint of 10Publishing. content: By Mark Ellis – As a 10-year-old boy, Mark Davidson’s mother gave him Hal Lindsey’s book, The Late Great Planet Earth , which eventually sold some 35 million copies, and was declared the bestselling nonfiction book of the 1970s by the New York Times. The book had a great impact on Davidson and shaped his earliest views about end times Bible prophecy. Shaken by the events of 9/11, Davidson, a retired aerospace engineer, dug more deeply into end-times prophecy, seeking answers about the direction of world events.  As he dove into Scripture related to prophecy, he developed a framework that diverges from traditional teaching in several ways, and resulted in his book: Daniel Revisited : Discovering the Four Mideast Signs Leading to the Antichrist. The most relevant of his teaching to current events is his view of Iran. Based on his study of Daniel 7, Daniel 8 and Revelation 6, Davidson identified four major events, which he calls “signposts,” that he believes will unfold in the Middle East before the Tribulation. The second signpost involves Iran (Shia) attacking its Sunni neighbors. “At some point, Iran will destroy the rest of the Arab oil infrastructure of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the UAE, Qatar, and Iraq,” Davidson predicts, based on his interpretation. “They’ve told the U.S. and Israel, if you attack and destroy our energy infrastructure, we’re going to do the same to all the other neighboring countries.” The attacks could be imminent, based on statements by leaders on both sides. “Iran’s threatening to do this prior to November 3 rd as an October surprise, and Trump is threatening to attack after the midterm elections. “So it could actually be quite soon where it blows up. But that’s what I see happening: the U.S. and Israel would attack Iran. title: Patrick Nagatani: The Spiritual Search Through Color, Photography, and Art
summary: Arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 2009, I was fortunate to catch the final chapter of artist and photographer Patrick Nagatani’s remarkable career before his death from cancer in 2017. As one of my favorite modern photographers, Nagatani fascinated me with his unique artistic vision, his imaginative compositions, and his ability to transform his photography […]  The post  Patrick Nagatani: The Spiritual Search Through Color, Photography, and Art  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: Arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 2009, I was fortunate to catch the final chapter of artist and photographer Patrick Nagatani’ s remarkable career before his death from cancer in 2017. As one of my favorite modern photographers, Nagatani fascinated me with his unique artistic vision, his imaginative compositions, and his ability to transform his photography into extraordinary works of art. Watching him at gallery openings was a pleasure. He was cordial, kind, and genuinely responsive to those who engaged him. There was something refreshing about an artist of his stature who remained approachable, thoughtful, and seemingly delighted to discuss his work. An Artist Shaped by History Photo credit: Grahm Howe, 1979. Patrick Ryoichi Nagatani was born on August 19, 1945, in Chicago, Illinois, only days after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. His Japanese American parents had experienced incarceration during World War II, and the legacy of displacement, cultural identity, and nuclear destruction would profoundly influence his artistic imagination. Raised Catholic, Nagatani eventually moved with his family to Los Angeles. He studied at UCLA, earning his Master of Fine Arts in 1980. His early professional experience included model-making for Hollywood productions, helping establish the theatrical techniques that later distinguished his photography. In 1987, he moved to Albuquerque to teach at the University of New Mexico , where he became an influential professor and internationally recognized artist. His celebrated Nuclear Enchantment series examined the disturbing relationship between New Mexico’s landscapes and the nuclear industry. Other projects investigated Japanese American incarceration, archaeology, cultural memory, and the uncertainty of photographic truth. ‘Generation to Generation’, Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) Nuclear Powered Vehicles, West Mesa, Albuquerque, New Mexico, 1991 & 1993, Chromogenic print (Ilfocolor Deluxe), 17 X 22 and 27 3/4 X 34 1/4 My interest in Nagatani extends beyond the artistry of his photographs—the theatrical tableaux, vibrant colors, and beautifully constructed compositions—to what I perceive as an underlying spiritual search. Throughout his career, questions of identity, mortality, healing, and transcendence surfaced repeatedly. Though not every work was explicitly religious, I suggest that there’s a longing to discover meaning beyond the material world. One early example is his series Colorful Cathedrals (1980–1983), which invites consideration of the relationship between artistic creation and spiritual imagination. Colorful Cathedrals: Light and the Sacred Nagatani’s Colorful Cathedrals emerged during his early experimentation with color photography and constructed imagery. The series was exhibited in Los Angeles and elsewhere, including a 1983 exhibition at the Arco Center for Visual Arts. His artistic practice during this period involved manipulating photographic environments rather than merely documenting existing scenes. Using constructed arrangements, controlled lighting, and photographic experimentation, he explored how color could transform visual experience. Canterbury #1, Kent, England, 1981, 36 X 33 X 2 1/2, nine P-12 Cibachrome prints from original SX-70’s with mixed media (oils, enamels, watercolors, sprayed and selectively hand colored) For me, the title of the series suggests something spiritually evocative. Cathedrals have historically served as architectural expressions of Christian theology, with light and color—particularly through stained glass—symbolizing divine illumination. Having graduated at Canterbury Christchurch University, with an Evensong service at Canterbury Cathedral, I’m drawn to his “Canterbury #1” work. Patrick Nagatani juxtaposes the grandeur of a Gothic cathedral with human hands holding yellow cards, suggesting a tension between sacred architecture and humanity’s search for spiritual meaning.
